questions.q: Why can't a before-save Apex trigger or before-save Flow make a callout to validate an address?
options: Because address validation APIs don't support JSON
Because a before-save context already has DML pending as part of that same save, and a callout can't run while DML is pending in the same transaction
Because Flow can never make HTTP callouts under any circumstance
Because before-save triggers run asynchronously already
questions.explain: This is the same transaction-ordering rule from Lesson 7 — a before-save context has pending DML, which blocks any callout in that same transaction.

questions.q: What is Option A in this lesson's design, and when does it fit?
options: An after-insert trigger enqueuing a Queueable; fits bulk API imports
A Screen Flow with an HTTP Callout action, validating the address while the user is still on the screen before any DML occurs; fits interactive, human-driven entry
A Batch Apex job run nightly; fits large-volume reconciliation
A custom Apex SOAP web service; fits legacy systems
questions.explain: Option A validates before any save happens at all, using a Screen Flow callout during the interactive session — there's no before-save DML conflict because no save has occurred yet.

questions.q: In Option B, why is it safe for the AddressValidationJob's Queueable to make a callout and then update the Contact, when the original project couldn't do this synchronously?
options: Because the trigger is an after-insert trigger, so the Contact's own creation DML has already committed by the time the Queueable's callout runs
Because Queueable Apex is exempt from all governor limits
Because the Contact object has no required fields
Because Option B never actually performs any DML
questions.explain: The after-insert trigger's own DML has already completed before the Queueable even runs, so the callout-then-DML sequence inside the Queueable's own fresh transaction doesn't violate the ordering rule.

questions.q: When does this lesson recommend using Option A, Option B, or both?
options: Option A should always replace Option B entirely
Option A fits interactive entry where feedback adds value; Option B fits non-interactive creation paths; many real systems need both to cover all creation paths
Option B should never be used since it introduces a delay
Both options are functionally identical and interchangeable
questions.explain: Option A gives interactive feedback during entry, while Option B catches records created without a user present (like API imports) — many real implementations need both as complementary safety nets.

questions.q: What pattern (from Lesson 18-19) does this entire project illustrate?
options: Fire and Forget
Request-Reply, since the validation result is needed before the Contact's address is considered verified
Batch Data Synchronization
Remote Call-In
questions.explain: The validation result is a required answer the process needs before considering the address complete, matching the Request-Reply pattern even though the implementation has to work around the before-save callout constraint.
